questions.q: What has IBM's superconducting quantum computing roadmap particularly emphasized?
options: Modularity -- connecting multiple smaller quantum chips together as a path to higher total qubit counts, alongside a multi-year roadmap of growing qubit counts (on the order of hundreds in recent years, roughly)
Focusing exclusively on single monolithic chips with no modular connections
Abandoning superconducting qubits entirely in favor of trapped ions
Avoiding any form of cloud access to its hardware
questions.explain: IBM has been explicit about pursuing modularity -- linking smaller chips together -- as part of a roadmap toward larger total qubit counts, rather than relying solely on ever-larger single chips.

questions.q: What has Google's superconducting quantum computing effort been particularly associated with?
options: Avoiding superconducting qubits in favor of a different hardware type entirely
Quantum supremacy/advantage demonstrations and significant investment in surface-code quantum error correction research
Exclusively commercial cloud sales with no research publications
Being the only company to never publish any quantum computing research
questions.explain: Google is particularly known for headline supremacy-style experiments and for its surface-code error correction research, which the lesson argues matters more long-term than any single supremacy demonstration.

questions.q: How does the lesson describe Rigetti's position relative to IBM and Google?
options: A smaller commercial footprint, with a multi-chip approach to scaling and more direct positioning as a commercial cloud-accessible quantum computing vendor
A company that does not build superconducting qubits at all
The largest of the three companies by funding and qubit count
A government-only supplier with no commercial customers
questions.explain: Rigetti has a meaningfully smaller footprint than IBM or Google and has leaned toward a multi-chip scaling approach and commercial cloud access, rather than competing primarily on raw qubit-count headlines.

questions.q: Why does the lesson caution against using raw qubit count alone to rank these companies' hardware?
options: Because all three companies always report exactly the same qubit count
Because qubit count is not a real, measurable property of a quantum chip
Because qubit count only matters for classical computers, not quantum ones

Because qubit count, coherence time, gate fidelity, and connectivity all trade off against each other, so more qubits with worse coherence or connectivity can be less useful than fewer, better-connected, lower-error qubits
questions.explain: A chip's real usefulness depends on several properties trading off against each other -- a higher qubit count with worse coherence, fidelity, or connectivity does not automatically make a chip more capable for real computation.

questions.q: What fundamental physical limitations does the lesson say IBM, Google, and Rigetti's superconducting processors all still share, despite their different strategies?
options: Finite coherence times limiting circuit depth, limited fixed connectivity between neighboring qubits, and the cryostat wiring bottleneck limiting practical qubit counts
A complete inability to run any quantum circuit longer than one gate
None -- each company has fully solved coherence, connectivity, and wiring limitations with a different proprietary method
A shared requirement to operate at room temperature
questions.explain: Despite different strategic choices, all three companies' superconducting processors are still bounded by the same core physical limitations covered earlier in the chapter: coherence time, connectivity, and cryostat wiring constraints.
